rect.title: <b>ACCPPDE101 Personal & Professional Development</b><br>This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal<br>development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate<br>oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of<br>core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent<br>learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills<br>and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on<br>societal issues and engage with societal partners.

<b>BENBUSI311 Transnational Business Law</b><br>Businesses and entrepreneurs are confronted with legal complexity not only at<br>the domestic level but particularly across divergent legal systems. This course<br>presents a survey of the most essential fields of business law: contracts<br>law, company law, trade law, intellectual property, and dispute resolution. An<br>ultimate aim of the course is to critically examine the impact of globalization<br>and digitization on the development of business law.

<b>BENBUSI312 Money, Banking & Finance</b><br>We study financial markets (stocks, bonds, derivatives) and financial<br>institutions (commercial banks and central banks). We address such questions as:<br>Can you outperform the stock market? Why are banks inherently fragile? What do<br>central banks do? What causes financial crises? Throughout the semester, student<br>teams participate in a business simulation, the Stanford Banking Game. Each team<br>manages a virtual bank and tries to maximize its share price.

<b>BENENTR212 Strategy & Digital Transformation</b><br>The course explores how companies develop strategies and drive responsible<br>digital transformation amid rapid technology change impacting the economy<br>and society. Students develop a strategic plan, from vision to execution, and<br>identify digital value opportunities. Using industry cases, they gain foresight<br>into digital technologies and their impact on strategy, business models and<br>social responsibilities.

<b>BENENTR311 Market Research</b><br>See how companies figure out what customers love and what they don’t. You’ll<br>plan and carry out real research, analyze what you find, and share your results.<br>Our course shows you how to gather opinions and turn them into smart business<br>ideas. Ready to turn curiosity into career skills? Perfect for future marketers,<br>analysts, or entrepreneurs.

<b>BENENTR312 International Business & Governance</b><br>This course examines the institutional, political and cultural forces shaping<br>global businesses. It first explores how international companies operate,<br>then centers on key global challenges including cross-border governance,<br>corporate responsibility, geopolitical strategies and global trade. It provides<br>a comprehensive understanding of today’s complex international business<br>environment.

<b>BENECON211 International Macroeconomics</b><br>Study the economy as a whole through topics such as national income, economic<br>growth, inflation, and unemployment. Understand how governments and central<br>banks use fiscal and monetary policies to influence economic performance<br>over time. The course also explores business cycles, international trade,<br>and economic crises, preparing students to evaluate policy debates and global<br>economic trends.

<b>BENECON212 Microeconomics & Behavior</b><br>Study how consumers and producers make decisions under scarcity. Explore<br>key concepts such as rational choice, decision-making under uncertainty, and<br>non-egoistic preferences. Analyze market structures, strategic interactions, and<br>factor markets. Learn how markets function and examine the impact of regulation.<br>Develop analytical tools to better understand behavior and engage with empirical<br>research.

<b>BENECON311 Public Economics</b><br>Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public<br>policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public<br>goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with<br>empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.

<b>BENECON312 Econometrics</b><br>Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and<br>prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares,<br>Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test,<br>F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly<br>the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo<br>simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic<br>relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.

<b>BENECON314 Behavioral Economics</b><br>This course integrates insights from psychology into economic theory to better<br>understand how people make decisions. Learn how actual behavior deviates from<br>the predictions of traditional economic models due to biases, heuristics,<br>and framing. Through experiments, students will deepen their understanding of<br>decision-making and its implications for economic theory and practice.

<b>BENENTR211 Marketing & Consumer Engagement</b><br>This course unpacks what drives consumer engagement with brands and how<br>marketers build customer trust responsibly. It introduces key marketing<br>concepts, consumer psychology, AI/technology-driven marketing innovation,<br>and brand and communication strategies. Students will explore real-life case<br>studies, develop a strategic marketing plan and learn how marketers build<br>sustainable brand strategies.

<b>BENLEAD211 Psychology of Leading Under Pressure</b><br>What does it take to lead effectively through pressure, conflict, and diversity?<br>Explore how emotion, identity, belonging, and inclusion shape leadership,<br>teamwork, and performance. Design and conduct an original empirical study<br>while building career-ready skills in research design, data analysis, teamwork,<br>ethical decision-making, and scientific communication.

<b>BENLEAD311 Psychology of Organizations & Leadership</b><br>This course offers Liberal Arts and Sciences students a deep dive into the<br>psychological, social, and structural dynamics that shape workplaces. Through<br>interactive case discussions, simulations, and real-world insights, students<br>develop critical skills in motivation, leadership, group dynamics, and culture.<br>By synthesizing research and applying theory to practice, participants gain the<br>tools to navigate and influence diverse organizational environments effectively.

<b>BENLEAD312 Negotiation & Strategic Thinking</b><br>How do you get to yes? In this course you will learn how to craft persuasive<br>arguments, deploy the right language, negotiate more effectively, and influence<br>decisions with confidence—whether in business, leadership, or life.

<b>BENBUSI112 Accounting & Corporate Finance</b><br>This course describes the most widely accepted accounting theory and practice<br>with an emphasis on using and analyzing the information in financial statements.<br>Students learn how to comprehend a typical corporate annual report and to use<br>accounting as a tool in understanding how economic events affect business.

<b>BENBUSI211 Business & Economy in the Age of AI</b><br>This course includes a multi-faceted exploration of AI’s business, managerial,<br>economic and related societal implications. Designed for students with a strong<br>interest in AI, it requires no prior technical background.

<b>BENECON111 Introduction to Economics</b><br>Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This<br>course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics,<br>including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and<br>provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.

<b>BENENTR111 Consumer Product Design</b><br>You will learn how to function in a ‘real-world’ design and development team<br>for consumer products. We go through the phases of design and development:<br>probe customer needs, translate these into a product concept, develop a<br>fabrication method, analyze sustainability, analyze costs and proceeds. Design<br>and development involves interviewing customers, brainstorming, laboratory<br>experiments, quantitative modeling, constructing a prototype, and considering<br>protection of intellectual property.

<b>BENLEAD111 Personal Leadership</b><br>Personal Leadership provides a comprehensive introduction to leadership theory<br>and practice, designed to help students discover their unique leadership<br>style through self-awareness and practical skill-building. Through interactive<br>workshops, reflective exercises, and real-world applications, students engage<br>deeply with core leadership principles and develop the tools needed to lead<br>confidently in any setting.

<b>BENLEAD112 Leadership Communication</b><br>This course blends theory with practice from both fiction and the real world,<br>helping you develop essential leadership skills. Learn how to inspire teams,<br>sharpen your communication, take ethical decisions, and lead with confidence.

rect.title: <b>BENGATE101 Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations</b><br>Through experiential learning, students turn their own bold ideas into new<br>ventures. No prior business expertise is required as teams work on a startup<br>project from ideation to final pitch while gaining business and entrepreneurial<br>skills in areas such as design thinking, business model and customer validation.<br>The class fosters creativity and collaboration to drive business and social<br>innovation.

<b>BENGATE102 Research Methods & Statistics</b><br>Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business<br>management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to<br>true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically,<br>from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey<br>techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a<br>brief intro to multivariate tools.

<b>DISARIN211 Decision-making in AI</b><br>Introduces planning techniques for AI systems in deterministic and<br>non‑deterministic environments. Addresses uncertainty, partial observability,<br>resource planning and optimizing behaviour under constraints.

<b>DISARIN311 Optimization Methods in AI</b><br>Covers computational methods for search problems in complex and adversarial<br>environments. Includes uninformed and informed search, local and global search,<br>adversarial games and constraint satisfaction problems.

<b>DISARIN312 Reinforcement Learning</b><br>Explores reinforcement learning. Covers theoretical frameworks and algorithms<br>and requires students to implement algorithms and build agents using neural<br>networks that learn through trial and error.

<b>DISCOMP211 Networks & Operating Systems</b><br>Introduces computer networks and operating systems. Covers how the internet<br>works and the role of an OS in resource management and application support.

<b>DISCOMP213 Software Development</b><br>Covers software design, creation, testing and maintenance. Uses C++ and Haskell<br>and covers planning, requirements gathering, testing, deployment and maintenance<br>through discussions and code reviews.

<b>DISCOMP311 Algorithms & Data Structures</b><br>Teaches design and analysis of algorithms and data structures, emphasizing<br>performance analysis and focusing on prominent algorithms and data structures.
<b>DISCOMP312 Advanced Algorithms</b><br>Studies modern algebraic algorithms and optimization methods. Emphasises<br>algorithmic thinking and mathematical modelling of computational problems.

<b>DISDATA311 Neural Networks & Deep Learning</b><br>Explores theory and practice of neural networks. Students build basic networks<br>and progress to complex networks for computer vision, and discuss recent<br>developments in large language and image generation models.
<b>DISDATA312 Robotics</b><br>Covers computational problems in robotics. Includes forward and inverse<br>kinematics, motion planning, collision avoidance and robotic grasping and<br>manipulation.

<b>DISMATH211 Linear Algebra</b><br>Introduces systems of equations, vectors, matrices and linear spaces with<br>emphasis on visual and conceptual understanding. Applies concepts across fields<br>and includes hands‑on exercises using computer algebra software.

<b>DISMATH213 Computational & Numerical Methods</b><br>Introduces numerical methods such as root‑finding, interpolation, numerical<br>differentiation and integration and solving differential equations. Emphasises<br>algorithm accuracy, stability and efficiency and uses computer algebra software.

<b>DISMATH214 Advanced Calculus</b><br>Extends elementary calculus to multiple dimensions and differential equations,<br>including complex‑valued functions. Uses computer algebra software to deepen<br>analytical skills for science and data analysis applications.

<b>DISMATH312 Linear Systems</b><br>Focuses on analysis of linear systems from an engineering perspective. Explores<br>representations via differential equations, transfer functions, state‑space and<br>signal‑flow diagrams and discusses applications in control, signal processing<br>and modelling.

<b>DISMATH314 Probability & Statistics</b><br>Provides a foundation in mathematical statistics. Covers probability theory,<br>discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and<br>simulation; uses computer algebra software to develop theoretical understanding<br>and practical skills.

<b>DISARIN111 AI Ethics</b><br>Explores philosophical foundations and implications of AI. Examines the history<br>of AI, ethical issues like interpretability, bias and alignment, debates about<br>AI consciousness and implications for human nature.

<b>DISARIN212 Logic & Discrete Mathematics</b><br>Focuses on mathematics of decision‑making, covering topics in discrete<br>mathematics such as logic, patterns and structures, with applications to<br>computer science and algorithm construction.
<b>DISCOMP212 Database Management Systems</b><br>Introduces relational database management systems and SQL. Covers relational<br>database theory, authorization, normalization and query processing.

<b>DISDATA111 Introduction to Data Science</b><br>Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation.<br>Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from<br>various disciplines.

<b>DISDATA211 Machine Learning</b><br>Covers core machine learning techniques from linear regression to advanced<br>tree‑based methods. Discusses strengths and weaknesses and applies methods to<br>real data from fields like medicine, physics and economics.

<b>DISDATA212 Image Processing & Computer Vision</b><br>Covers processing and analysis of image data, including feature detection and<br>tracking. Discusses applications in medicine, self‑driving vehicles, gaming,<br>robotics and traffic management.

rect.title: <b>DISGATE101 Introduction to Programming</b><br>Introduces programming and computer science. Covers structured programming, data<br>constructs, testing, debugging and object‑oriented programming with Python, and<br>develops computational problem‑solving skills.

<b>DISGATE102 Mathematical Methods</b><br>Introduces linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues) and calculus (limits,<br>differentiation, integration) to construct and solve equations. Provides<br>problem‑solving skills applicable across disciplines.

<b>ENSENVI211 Earth Observation</b><br>Provides hands‑on experience with GIS and data integration using geospatial data<br>from satellites and drones. Uncovers how human actions impact ecosystems and<br>climate and promotes sustainable practices through research projects.

<b>ENSENVI213 Earth System Science Tools</b><br>Explores interactions among biosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and atmosphere.<br>Teaches system modelling, uses proxies and isotope tracers to study past and<br>future climates and includes a field trip focused on greenhouse gas pathways.

<b>ENSENVI311 Environmental Biogeochemistry</b><br>Investigates natural waters and their interactions with rocks, soils and<br>minerals. Examines biogeochemical processes and cycles, including weathering,<br>mineral formation, absorption, water treatment and resource recovery; utilises<br>geochemical modelling and a case study.

<b>ENSSUST211 Energy & Sustainability</b><br>Introduces renewable energy resources and technologies, discussing<br>environmental, political and economic constraints. Covers energy storage and<br>demand management and aims to balance energy supply and demand.

<b>ENSDELT311 R3: Recycling, Recovery, Remediation</b><br>Examines strategies and technologies towards a circular economy. Explores<br>resource security and stewardship, develops lab skills and inorganic chemistry<br>knowledge, and connects to themes at the Delta Climate Center.

<b>ENSENVI312 Earth's Resources</b><br>Provides in‑depth geoscience research into resource and environmental challenges<br>such as nuclear waste storage, geothermal energy and CO₂ capture. Students<br>conduct literature reviews and produce class reports for presentation to a<br>professional conference.

<b>ENSSUST311 Renewable System Design</b><br>Teaches assessment of energy usage patterns and strategies for reducing<br>consumption or transitioning to cleaner energy. Explores solar, wind and<br>bioenergy solutions and includes technical and economic analysis; students<br>deliver a report and presentation to a partner company.

<b>ENSSUST315 Spatial Planning</b><br>Explores spatial engineering and geospatial technologies like GIS and remote<br>sensing for addressing global challenges such as natural disasters, food<br>shortages, resource decline and pollution. Emphasises hands‑on projects in<br>disaster response, sustainable agriculture and environmental monitoring.

<b>ENSDELT111 Building with Nature</b><br>Introduces the sustainable engineering approach of working with natural<br>processes for flood protection, land reclamation and port development. Covers<br>history and principles of ecosystem‑based design, explores case studies and<br>includes guest lectures and field excursions.

<b>ENSDELT211 Living with Water</b><br>Explores sustainable water management in delta regions. Focuses on adaptation<br>to rising seas, floods and land subsidence; engages students in projects in<br>Zeeland; and highlights nature‑based solutions and resilient infrastructure.

<b>ENSDELT312 Governance of Sustainability</b><br>This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process<br>of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental<br>and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016).<br>Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on<br>the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors<br>represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion<br>on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at<br>the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end<br>of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of<br>the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical<br>and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.

<b>ENSECOL111 Introduction to Biodiversity</b><br>The biosphere consists of millions of living species. In this course we will<br>travel through the tree of life, starting with bacteria and single-celled<br>eukaryotes such as reef-building dinoflagellates and disease-causing<br>apicomplexans. Next, we will look at the multicellular groups: plants, seaweeds,<br>fungi and animals. We will also investigate the relevance of biodiversity for<br>human society in fields such as food and food security, economy, climate and<br>health.

<b>ENSECOL112 Conservation Biology</b><br>This course explores environmental conservation through biological and social<br>science perspectives. Topics include biodiversity importance, threats to<br>ecosystems, conservation methods, and tools to monitor and protect nature. It<br>also covers national and international laws, policies, and initiatives aimed at<br>preserving ecosystems and ensuring a sustainable future for current and future<br>generations.

<b>ENSECOL211 The Science of Evolution</b><br>Evolution is the unifying theory in biology. As such, an understanding of<br>evolutionary biology is vital for understanding the natural world. In this<br>course, we will discuss key concepts in evolution such as population genetics,<br>variation and selection, speciation, macro-evolution and the origins of life.<br>The importance of evolutionary concepts to all other fields of biology will<br>be emphasized, as well as important implications of evolutionary processes in<br>fields like human health and climate change.

<b>ENSECOL212 Ecosystems Uncovered: How Nature Works</b><br>Focuses on basic principles of ecology. Studies how environmental conditions<br>affect organisms and examines ecological principles governing individuals,<br>populations, communities and ecosystems, including ecological modelling and<br>applied case studies.

<b>ENSECOL311 Marine Biology</b><br>Studies ecological processes in marine environments such as estuaries, rocky<br>shores and coral reefs. Examines human impacts and includes guest lectures, lab<br>visits, excursions and field work, culminating in an essay.

<b>ENSECOL312 Sustainable Farming & Innovation</b><br>Discusses environmental impacts of agriculture and explores sustainable<br>agriculture approaches such as agroecology, organic farming, conservation<br>agriculture, precision agriculture, sustainable livestock farming, agroforestry,<br>permaculture, crop rotation, integrated pest management and sustainable supply<br>chains.

<b>ENSENVI111 Dynamic Earth</b><br>Introduces Earth Science by focusing on interactions among the deep earth,<br>lithosphere and hydrosphere. Highlights key cycles shaping Earth’s surface and<br>includes indoor/outdoor labs and a multi‑day field excursion.

<b>ENSENVI112 Natural Hazards, Risks & Adaptations</b><br>Covers geoscience principles and analytical tools to understand natural<br>disasters. Compares risks from climate change‑driven events and mining disasters<br>and teaches actions to reduce risks from events like earthquakes, droughts and<br>toxic algae blooms.

<b>ENSENVI212 Soils & Aquifers</b><br>Explores soils and aquifers through fieldwork and lab analyses. Covers soil<br>formation, properties, health and remediation and investigates mapping aquifers<br>for geothermal energy, coastal defence and freshwater resource assessment.

<b>ENSSUST111 Climate Change</b><br>Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea<br>level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. Discusses adaptation and<br>mitigation solutions, including renewable energy systems, carbon storage and<br>climate‑adaptive planning, and examines climate governance and justice.

<b>ENSSUST112 Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy</b><br>Teaches evaluation of environmental impacts of products, processes and services<br>throughout their lifecycle. Emphasises strategic planning for a circular economy<br>through hands‑on learning.

<b>ENSSUST113 Calling Bullshit</b><br>Develops skills to recognise and handle misinformation. Discusses cognitive<br>biases and detection methods, distinguishes real from fake experts, and includes<br>case studies and a video project tackling a misinformation topic.

<b>ENSSUST313 Research in a Sustainable Delta</b><br>In this project course you will work in small teams of two or three students<br>on a research problem relevant for sustainability in the broadest sense. We<br>are looking for collaborations with local companies and other institutions. The<br>research questions are supplied by a regional institution or company that is<br>active in areas related to sustainability in the broadest sense. In this way<br>it is guaranteed that the research projects are indeed relevant for the Zeeland<br>delta. Furthermore, students will have access to expertise and/or facilities of<br>the external partner, which will broaden their perspective. Usually, there will<br>be one person affiliated with the external partner organization involved with a<br>project team as external advisor

text.title: <b>ENSENVI211 Earth Observation</b><br>Provides hands‑on experience with GIS and data integration using geospatial data<br>from satellites and drones. Uncovers how human actions impact ecosystems and<br>climate and promotes sustainable practices through research projects.

<b>ENSENVI213 Earth System Science Tools</b><br>Explores interactions among biosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and atmosphere.<br>Teaches system modelling, uses proxies and isotope tracers to study past and<br>future climates and includes a field trip focused on greenhouse gas pathways.

<b>ENSENVI311 Environmental Biogeochemistry</b><br>Investigates natural waters and their interactions with rocks, soils and<br>minerals. Examines biogeochemical processes and cycles, including weathering,<br>mineral formation, absorption, water treatment and resource recovery; utilises<br>geochemical modelling and a case study.

<b>ENSSUST211 Energy & Sustainability</b><br>Introduces renewable energy resources and technologies, discussing<br>environmental, political and economic constraints. Covers energy storage and<br>demand management and aims to balance energy supply and demand.

<b>ENSDELT311 R3: Recycling, Recovery, Remediation</b><br>Examines strategies and technologies towards a circular economy. Explores<br>resource security and stewardship, develops lab skills and inorganic chemistry<br>knowledge, and connects to themes at the Delta Climate Center.

<b>ENSENVI312 Earth's Resources</b><br>Provides in‑depth geoscience research into resource and environmental challenges<br>such as nuclear waste storage, geothermal energy and CO₂ capture. Students<br>conduct literature reviews and produce class reports for presentation to a<br>professional conference.

<b>ENSSUST311 Renewable System Design</b><br>Teaches assessment of energy usage patterns and strategies for reducing<br>consumption or transitioning to cleaner energy. Explores solar, wind and<br>bioenergy solutions and includes technical and economic analysis; students<br>deliver a report and presentation to a partner company.

<b>ENSSUST315 Spatial Planning</b><br>Explores spatial engineering and geospatial technologies like GIS and remote<br>sensing for addressing global challenges such as natural disasters, food<br>shortages, resource decline and pollution. Emphasises hands‑on projects in<br>disaster response, sustainable agriculture and environmental monitoring.

<b>ENSDELT111 Building with Nature</b><br>Introduces the sustainable engineering approach of working with natural<br>processes for flood protection, land reclamation and port development. Covers<br>history and principles of ecosystem‑based design, explores case studies and<br>includes guest lectures and field excursions.

<b>ENSDELT211 Living with Water</b><br>Explores sustainable water management in delta regions. Focuses on adaptation<br>to rising seas, floods and land subsidence; engages students in projects in<br>Zeeland; and highlights nature‑based solutions and resilient infrastructure.

<b>ENSDELT312 Governance of Sustainability</b><br>This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process<br>of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental<br>and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016).<br>Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on<br>the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors<br>represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion<br>on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at<br>the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end<br>of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of<br>the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical<br>and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.

<b>ENSECOL111 Introduction to Biodiversity</b><br>The biosphere consists of millions of living species. In this course we will<br>travel through the tree of life, starting with bacteria and single-celled<br>eukaryotes such as reef-building dinoflagellates and disease-causing<br>apicomplexans. Next, we will look at the multicellular groups: plants, seaweeds,<br>fungi and animals. We will also investigate the relevance of biodiversity for<br>human society in fields such as food and food security, economy, climate and<br>health.

<b>ENSECOL112 Conservation Biology</b><br>This course explores environmental conservation through biological and social<br>science perspectives. Topics include biodiversity importance, threats to<br>ecosystems, conservation methods, and tools to monitor and protect nature. It<br>also covers national and international laws, policies, and initiatives aimed at<br>preserving ecosystems and ensuring a sustainable future for current and future<br>generations.

<b>ENSECOL211 The Science of Evolution</b><br>Evolution is the unifying theory in biology. As such, an understanding of<br>evolutionary biology is vital for understanding the natural world. In this<br>course, we will discuss key concepts in evolution such as population genetics,<br>variation and selection, speciation, macro-evolution and the origins of life.<br>The importance of evolutionary concepts to all other fields of biology will<br>be emphasized, as well as important implications of evolutionary processes in<br>fields like human health and climate change.

<b>ENSECOL212 Ecosystems Uncovered: How Nature Works</b><br>Focuses on basic principles of ecology. Studies how environmental conditions<br>affect organisms and examines ecological principles governing individuals,<br>populations, communities and ecosystems, including ecological modelling and<br>applied case studies.

<b>ENSECOL311 Marine Biology</b><br>Studies ecological processes in marine environments such as estuaries, rocky<br>shores and coral reefs. Examines human impacts and includes guest lectures, lab<br>visits, excursions and field work, culminating in an essay.

Compares risks from climate change‑driven events and mining disasters<br>and teaches actions to reduce risks from events like earthquakes, droughts and<br>toxic algae blooms.

We<br>are looking for collaborations with local companies and other institutions. The<br>research questions are supplied by a regional institution or company that is<br>active in areas related to sustainability in the broadest sense. In this way<br>it is guaranteed that the research projects are indeed relevant for the Zeeland<br>delta. Furthermore, students will have access to expertise and/or facilities of<br>the external partner, which will broaden their perspective. Usually, there will<br>be one person affiliated with the external partner organization involved with a<br>project team as external advisor

rect.title: <b>ENSGATE101 Sustainability Essentials I</b><br>Provides key concepts in physics, chemistry, materials science, mathematics and<br>modelling necessary for sustainability. Uses a case study to connect concepts<br>to real‑world sustainability challenges and prepares students for 200‑level<br>sustainability courses.

<b>ENSGATE201 Sustainability Essentials II</b><br>Builds on Sustainability Essentials I. Applies tools and knowledge to a<br>real‑world sustainability case study and allows students to delve deeper into<br>aspects connected to their field of interest.

<b>GOSLAWJ211 Criminal Law & Criminal Justice</b><br>Examines moral and legal justifications for criminalisation and punishment.<br>Investigates guiding principles of criminal law and justice, including criminal<br>accountability, guilt, legality and fundamental principles, and applies theory<br>through a simulated legal aid clinic.

<b>GOSLAWJ212 Introduction to Public International Law</b><br>Introduces rules, institutions and politics of public international law. Covers<br>treaties, the UN, armed conflict, war crimes, refugee protection and climate<br>change. Students analyse cases, debate issues and produce a podcast connecting<br>law to global challenges.

<b>GOSLAWJ213 Comparative Constitutional Law</b><br>Explores constitutional law and state organisation, using a comparative<br>approach. Covers constitutionalism, separation of powers, judicial review,<br>federalism and fundamental rights, and discusses constitution‑making, religious<br>constitutions and constitutional backsliding.

<b>GOSLAWJ311 Principles of Private Law</b><br>Examines principles of property law, tort law, contract law and other fields<br>within private law. Uses comparisons of legal systems in four countries to<br>explore rights and obligations arising from daily interactions.

<b>GOSLAWJ312 Foundations of European Union Law</b><br>Introduces the EU legal order. Studies institutions, framework, citizenship and<br>the internal market using problem‑based exercises and guest lectures.

<b>GOSHIST111 Modern History</b><br>Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses<br>industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination,<br>and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including<br>revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.

<b>GOSHIST112 Histories of Gender</b><br>Explores lives of ordinary people through the lens of gender from the 19th to<br>21st centuries. Uses storytelling across cultural forms; topics include slavery,<br>mid‑20th‑century life, conversion therapy, queer cinema and banned books;<br>engages with projects like Walking With Pride.

<b>GOSHIST211 History of Empires</b><br>Examines the rise and fall of empires and the contested concept of empire.<br>Discusses oppressive and benevolent features of empires, covers key theories on<br>empires and power politics and analyses major historical examples.

<b>GOSHIST213 Ways of War</b><br>Provides a chronological overview of warfare in the Western world from antiquity<br>to the present. Covers weapons, technology, strategy, defence, mercenaries,<br>cavalry, chivalry, Blitzkrieg, guerrilla warfare and nuclear arsenals,<br>illustrating competition for mastery in Western history.

<b>GOSHIST311 Native American Histories</b><br>This course introduces students to Native American history and life from the<br>19th through the 21st century. It argues that power, fear, misogyny, education,<br>genocide, and resilience shape the Indigenous past and present. Topics we<br>explore include the “Stolen Lives” of Indian children forcibly taken from their<br>homes and placed in Indian Boarding Schools from the 1830’s through the 1990’s;<br>Murdered and Missing Indigenous Women and Girls in the twenty-first century;<br>and the individual and community forms of cultural resistance and environmental<br>regeneration that connect past with present and future generations. We learn<br>from the Native American scholars and 2Spirit youth that speak to and with the<br>class. Exchange of cultural and intellectual knowledge also happens when we work<br>with Lakota students to address contemporary challenges. Legislation, memoir,<br>novels, and Indigenous children’s stories are central to our studies. So are the<br>analyses of contemporary music and artistic expressions and exhibitions, as well<br>as Hollywood and Indigenous film featuring Native American histories and lives.

<b>GOSHIST312 Researching the "American Century"</b><br>Guides students through the full arc of historical inquiry, from formulating<br>research questions to engaging critically with sources. Emphasises<br>methodological rigour and interdisciplinary thinking and culminates in a<br>substantial research paper.

<b>GOSLAWJ111 Human Rights: Law & Philosophy</b><br>Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies<br>classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines<br>the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights<br>treaties.

<b>GOSPHIL111 Introduction to Western Philosophy</b><br>Introduces central themes from Western philosophy over 2,500 years. Encourages<br>inquiry into the significance of philosophical issues and their relation to<br>other disciplines and teaches theoretical methods used by philosophers.

<b>GOSPHIL212 Ethics</b><br>Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology,<br>utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the<br>relation between happiness and pleasure. Applies theories to practical issues<br>such as animal rights, privacy, future generations, war, punishment, disability<br>and equality.

<b>GOSPHIL214 Philosophy of Mind</b><br>Examines historical and modern work on the philosophy of mind. Discusses<br>Descartes’ dualism, the nature of consciousness, AI and animal minds, personal<br>identity, transformative experiences and the influence of technology on<br>experience.

<b>GOSPHIL311 Philosophy of Emotion</b><br>Explores emotions from a philosophical perspective. Discusses nature and<br>rationality of emotions, their role in ethics and art, and draws on historical<br>and contemporary sources.

<b>GOSPHIL313 Free Will, Time & the Self</b><br>Investigates concepts of free will, the role of luck and openness of the future.<br>Explores relations between free will, time and the self across multiple modules<br>and contemporary debates.

<b>GOSPOLI111 Introduction to Political Philosophy</b><br>Introduces political philosophy. Examines concepts such as authority, freedom,<br>equality, democracy, human rights, pluralism, multiculturalism, poverty and<br>environmental issues through classical and contemporary texts. Emphasises essay<br>writing and presentations.

<b>GOSPOLI112 Foundations of Comparative Politics</b><br>Provides analytical tools to compare political systems and democracies. Examines<br>phenomena like democratic backsliding, decline of political parties, rise of<br>populism, media changes, non‑majoritarian institutions and globalization’s<br>impact on domestic politics.

<b>GOSPOLI212 Theory of International Relations</b><br>Introduces basic theories of international relations and applies them to<br>contemporary issues such as climate change, energy, humanitarian intervention,<br>global crises and international relations between North-South and South-South<br>actors. Includes a UN Security Council negotiation simulation.

<b>GOSPOLI311 European Union Politics</b><br>Introduces EU politics. Outlines actors, institutions and decision‑making<br>rules; examines responses to crises; and employs various approaches to study EU<br>politics and policy‑making.

<b>GOSPOLI312 Public Policy Analysis</b><br>Investigates public policy in the context of globalization. Uses a case study on<br>sugar to examine policy‑making phases and alternative conceptualisations across<br>national and international arenas. Students write policy memos.

<b>GOSPOLI313 Peace & Conflict</b><br>Introduces Peace & Conflict Studies. Examines definitions of peace and conflict;<br>analyzes conflict causation, violence typologies and radicalisation; applies<br>reconciliation and conflict‑transformation models to real‑world scenarios<br>through lectures and portfolio work.

<b>GOSSOCI111 Introduction to Sociology</b><br>Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines<br>socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois,<br>and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class<br>through theoretical approaches and methodologies.

<b>GOSSOCI212 Qualitative Research Methodology</b><br>Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions,<br>interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on<br>complexity and power dynamics in social research.

<b>GOSSOCI214 Modern Sociology</b><br>Examines the trajectory of sociology within the culture of imperialism and<br>colonial responses. Studies leading social theories and debates about modernity<br>and critically engages with sociological discourses.

<b>GOSSOCI215 Social Movements & Environmental Justice</b><br>Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case<br>studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such<br>as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to<br>encourage civic engagement.

<b>GOSSOCI311 New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory</b><br>Examines contemporary sociological debates about civil society through critical<br>tradition, neo‑functionalism and decolonial critiques. Includes research group<br>projects with NGOs or civil society organizations that translate conceptual<br>insights into empirical analysis.

rect.title: <b>GOSGATE102 Law, Society & Justice</b><br>Examines law from legal, socio‑scientific and normative perspectives. Explores<br>definitions, legal traditions and fields of law, investigates the relationship<br>between law and society and the concept of justice, and includes case law,<br>excursion to international legal organisations, interviews with practitioners<br>and a moot court session.

<b>HCBBIOM211 Functional Anatomy</b><br>Introduces human body functioning using imaging, surface anatomy and<br>dissection materials. Shows how anatomy serves function and discusses ethical<br>considerations of learning from the dead.

<b>HCBBIOM311 Pharmacology</b><br>Covers the science of drugs—their origin, composition, kinetics, therapeutic<br>use and toxicity. Discusses drug targets, interactions and kinetics, enabling<br>students to explain therapies in terms of molecular targets and physiological<br>consequences.

<b>HCBBIOM312 Infection & Immunity</b><br>Explores fundamental processes in immunology such as recognition of self<br>vs non‑self, lymphocyte receptor development and innate and adaptive immune<br>responses. Examines host‑pathogen interactions, inflammation, tissue damage and<br>immunopathology.

<b>HCBBIOM313 Mechanisms of Disease</b><br>Examines molecular and cellular defects triggering pathologies. Presents<br>clinical cases, discusses disease mechanisms and treatments across systems and<br>includes an assignment to invent an imaginary disease.

<b>HCBLIFE211 Molecular Cell Biology</b><br>Provides foundation for practical applications in life science. Focuses<br>on cellular biology of eukaryotes and prokaryotes, revisits concepts from<br>introductory courses, examines current research and encourages evaluating<br>reproducibility and modernising methods.

<b>HCBLIFE212 Human Physiology</b><br>Studies normal functioning of the human body, covering structure‑function<br>relationships, energy handling, homeostasis, signalling, organ systems and<br>integration of their functions.

<b>HCBLIFE213 Biochemistry</b><br>Explores the chemistry of life and biomolecules such as proteins, sugars,<br>lipids and nucleic acids. Discusses metabolic pathways, the role of biomolecules<br>in health and disease and applications in medicine, biotechnology and<br>sustainability.

<b>HCBLIFE214 Life Science Laboratory</b><br>Introduces biochemical and molecular laboratory work. Covers themes like<br>blood, proteins, bacteria, DNA and bioinformatics and provides a foundation for<br>clinical and biomedical research.

<b>HCBLIFE311 Molecular Pathology & Genetics</b><br>Covers general and molecular pathology and genetics. Studies cell injury, death,<br>inflammation, immunity, tissue repair, regeneration, fibrosis and neoplasia,<br>examines genetic mutations and diseases, and discusses genetic testing and<br>ethical considerations.

<b>HCBCOGN212 Perception & Action</b><br>Explores neural mechanisms behind perception and action. Examines how the brain<br>processes sensory information and guides goal‑directed behaviour using methods<br>from cognitive neuroscience and neuropsychology.

<b>HCBCOGN311 Higher Order Functions</b><br>Deepens understanding of neurophysiology and neuroanatomy. Explores higher‑level<br>cognitive functions—memory, emotion, social cognition, executive functioning and<br>language—and engages with current research while designing experiments.

<b>HCBCOGN312 Psycholinguistics</b><br>Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors<br>that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws<br>on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how<br>language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively,<br>on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental<br>issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the<br>relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition<br>of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to<br>the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity<br>as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language?<br>Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought;<br>aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics;<br>reading and dyslexia; speech production.

<b>HCBPSYC212 Psychopathology</b><br>The Psychopathology course offers a deep dive into the factors shaping mental<br>health across the lifespan. Students will develop critical thinking skills,<br>explore the bio-psycho-social approach, and gain a comprehensive understanding<br>of mental health and its disorders. Through key concepts, research findings, and<br>psychological assessment techniques, this course empowers individuals to promote<br>wellness and make a meaningful impact in both personal and professional spheres.

<b>HCBPSYC311 Medical & Health Psychology</b><br>Uses a biopsychosocial approach to explore how biological, psychological and<br>socio‑cultural factors influence health and illness. Covers theories, research<br>and interventions and focuses on the role of psychological expertise in medical<br>settings.

<b>HCBPSYC312 Psychodiagnostics & Psychotherapies</b><br>Introduces key theories, methods and practices in psychodiagnostics and<br>psychotherapy. Covers psychological assessment techniques and psychotherapeutic<br>approaches and builds practical competencies and clinical skills.

<b>HCBPSYC313 Advanced Research Methods & Statistics</b><br>This course guides you through combining results from multiple studies using<br>systematic reviews and meta-analysis a method now essential in psychology,<br>medicine, social science and other disciplines. Want to know what really works?<br>Gain hands-on skills in research synthesis that inform evidence-based policy<br>and practice. You’ll search literature, manage data, and present findings that<br>matter. Learn to calculate effect sizes, synthesize results and assess bias<br>using R.

<b>HCBPSYC314 Lifespan Developmental Psychology</b><br>Explores human development across the lifespan. Examines physical, cognitive,<br>emotional and social changes from prenatal life to old age and develops critical<br>thinking about factors influencing individual uniqueness.

<b>HCBBIOM111 Epidemiology & Public Health</b><br>Public health is about changing the world. From pandemics to lifestyle-related<br>diseases, from screening for disease to improving water and air quality, it<br>asks: how can we improve to keep the population healthy? But how do we know<br>what actually works? In this course you will dive into epidemiology: the science<br>behind public health. You will learn how to study disease, risks, and changes<br>over time, and how to critically evaluate evidence. Because behind every public<br>health decision lies a question of evidence, and by the end of this course, you<br>will be equipped to engage with it. This course invites you to look beyond the<br>lab, the hospital, and the library, into the wider world where health is shaped.<br>What matters most if we truly care about health, and how can we influence that?

<b>HCBCOGN112 Neurobiology</b><br>Examines evolution and complexity of brains. Explores animal cognition, welfare<br>and research ethics and studies how brain regions and rhythms regulate behaviour<br>through interactive assignments.

<b>HCBPSYC111 Social Psychology</b><br>Covers main theories, findings and principles of social psychology, emphasising<br>its scientific approach to understanding how people’s feelings, thoughts and<br>behaviour are influenced by the presence of others.

<b>HCBPSYC211 Statistics & Experimental Methods</b><br>The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in<br>psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in the medical<br>domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers<br>in other domains. In addition to technical training, the course emphasizes clear<br>academic communication. It will equip you with the skills necessary to apply<br>advanced statistical techniques to real-world research problems. With a focus<br>on practical application through case studies and data analysis projects, You<br>will be able to choose the appropriate statistical model for various research<br>scenarios and address common challenges in data interpretation.

<b>HCBPSYC315 Youth Resilience to Extremism</b><br>Interdisciplinary course combining psychology and other social sciences in which<br>students will have an opportunity to participate in an actual international<br>research project and develop evidence-based materials for youth leaders and<br>educators aimed at strengthening young people’s resilience to radicalization<br>by promoting democratic school culture, emotionally supportive learning<br>environments, empathy, civic engagement, and mental well-being.

text.title: <b>HCBBIOM211 Functional Anatomy</b><br>Introduces human body functioning using imaging, surface anatomy and<br>dissection materials. Shows how anatomy serves function and discusses ethical<br>considerations of learning from the dead.

<b>HCBBIOM311 Pharmacology</b><br>Covers the science of drugs—their origin, composition, kinetics, therapeutic<br>use and toxicity. Discusses drug targets, interactions and kinetics, enabling<br>students to explain therapies in terms of molecular targets and physiological<br>consequences.

<b>HCBBIOM312 Infection & Immunity</b><br>Explores fundamental processes in immunology such as recognition of self<br>vs non‑self, lymphocyte receptor development and innate and adaptive immune<br>responses. Examines host‑pathogen interactions, inflammation, tissue damage and<br>immunopathology.

<b>HCBBIOM313 Mechanisms of Disease</b><br>Examines molecular and cellular defects triggering pathologies. Presents<br>clinical cases, discusses disease mechanisms and treatments across systems and<br>includes an assignment to invent an imaginary disease.

<b>HCBLIFE211 Molecular Cell Biology</b><br>Provides foundation for practical applications in life science. Focuses<br>on cellular biology of eukaryotes and prokaryotes, revisits concepts from<br>introductory courses, examines current research and encourages evaluating<br>reproducibility and modernising methods.

rect.title: <b>HCBGATE101 Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine</b><br>Introduces biochemistry, macromolecules, cells, organ systems, DNA and cell<br>function. Connects fundamentals to health and disease and serves as a starting<br>point for medicine, biomedical science, life science or public health; no lab<br>experience needed.

<b>HCBGATE102 Introduction to Brain & Behavior</b><br>Explores why people behave as they do and how brain injuries affect mental<br>processes. Discusses nature and nurture, introduces brain anatomy and<br>psychological theories, and provides a gateway to cognitive science and clinical<br>psychology.

<b>MCCCOMM111 The Art of Rhetorical Communication</b><br>Teaches how to craft persuasive messages, influence opinions, inspire action and<br>connect people. Draws on historical communicators from Aristotle to Barack Obama<br>and applies stylistic techniques to students’ own writing and speaking.

<b>MCCCOMM112 Dutch</b><br>This course aims to develop basic skills and strategies necessary to<br>successfully handle uncomplicated oral and written communication in Dutch<br>in a variety of social situations that you may encounter in daily life in<br>the Netherlands. The emphasis in the course will be on speaking in Dutch in<br>day-to-day situations on the one hand and understanding Dutch culture on the<br>other hand. At the end of the course students can orally express and write<br>about themselves in Dutch, who they are, describe their family background, and<br>interact with others in a simple way.

<b>MCCCOMM211 Style & Meaning</b><br>Explores how linguistic choices inform meaning and interpretation in literary<br>and non-fiction contexts. Introduces theoretical frameworks for close reading<br>and addresses power dynamics, obligation, uncertainty and ideological undertones<br>in language.

<b>MCCCOMM212 Communicating the Climate Crisis</b><br>Examines how the climate crisis is communicated and contested. Analyzes texts,<br>films, exhibitions, protest art, slogans and social media alongside theory<br>and case studies, teaching students to dissect arguments and culminating in a<br>project where students enter the debate.

<b>MCCCOMM213 Rhetoric in Action</b><br>Develops persuasive speaking skills by applying rhetorical theory in the<br>real world. Students work with local primary school children, building<br>public-speaking skills and empowering them to find their voices.

<b>MCCCOMM311 Persuasive Communication</b><br>Explores ethical persuasion and climate communication. Students learn persuasive<br>communication models and frameworks and collaborate with climate scientists at<br>the Delta Climate Centre to produce sustainability messaging on water, food and<br>energy.

<b>MCCCOMM312 Creative Communication Laboratory</b><br>Explores meaning-making through creative expression. Students study and practice<br>poetic forms, experiment with sonic poetry, performance and other unconventional<br>forms of communication, engage with theoretical texts and produce their own<br>creative work.

<b>MCCHEAM111 Introduction to Western Art History</b><br>Provides an introduction to Western art history, tracing major artistic<br>movements from the late Middle Ages to the present. Through close study of<br>key paintings and their makers, students gain insight into evolving styles,<br>techniques and cultural influences.

<b>MCCHEAM112 Introduction to World Archaeology</b><br>Explores ancient craft production from around the world. Examines how making<br>objects shaped human development and how ancient solutions can inform modern<br>sustainability.

<b>MCCHEAM211 African Art & Heritage</b><br>Examines the artistic, historical and ethical dimensions of African art.<br>Highlights distinct forms and cultural significance, considers influence<br>on Western modernism and addresses looting, colonial-era acquisitions and<br>repatriation efforts.

<b>MCCHEAM212 Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean</b><br>This course examines the painting, sculpture, and architecture of Renaissance<br>Italy and the extensive artistic connections that linked the Italian peninsula<br>to other regions of the world. By exploring a range of geographical contexts,<br>from the Islamic courts of the Eastern Mediterranean and the commercial routes<br>connecting Europe, Asia, and Africa to the newly encountered territories of<br>the Americas, students will examine how trade, colonization, and cross-cultural<br>exchange shaped the production and meaning of Renaissance art.

<b>MCCHEAM213 Greek Archaeology</b><br>The invention of democracy in classical Greece changed the nature of community<br>decision-making, perhaps forever. This process is reflected in the material<br>culture of the period. By examining the archaeology of community & democracy in<br>early-democratic Greece, this course goes in search of ancient lessons for the<br>modern world.

<b>MCCHEAM312 Modern Art & Modern Museums</b><br>Examines debates on modern art through various themes. Focuses on the<br>relationship between art and its presentation in museums and exhibitions,<br>exploring curatorial practices and exhibition strategies.

<b>MCCHEAM315 Heritage & Ancient Democracy</b><br>In the modern world democracy is associated with participation, rationality and<br>freedom. In this course, we go back to the roots of democracy in ancient Greece,<br>when to a modern observer, it was not very democratic at all: foreigners, slaves<br>and women were excluded from elections and political decision-making. Even so,<br>the inclusion of all classes, also the poor, in politics was after antiquity<br>not achieved until the mid-nineteenth century. Ancient commentators criticised<br>Athenian democracy for being too extreme just because of this broad inclusion.<br>They argued that many were too uneducated, too emotional, and too irrational to<br>see through the cheap play on emotions by demagogues and would-be tyrants. This<br>course investigates how Athenian democracy was built, how it was intertwined<br>with myth and religion, and expressed in art, literature and architecture. It<br>traces the loci of democracy in archaeology, and analyses its temporary collapse<br>in the crisis of the late fifth century BC. Most importantly, we put ourselves<br>in our socio-political ancestors’ shoes by engaging in a simulation of the<br>Athenian assembly, in which we have to make decisions that will change our lives<br>forever. In doing so, we use the ancient heritage of democracy for an experiment<br>in applied sociology – to not only understand, but to feel the meaning of<br>political decision-making.

<b>MCCHEAM316 Writing Art's Histories</b><br>This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline,<br>tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth<br>century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by<br>figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault,<br>and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that<br>have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and<br>interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a<br>globalized world.

<b>MCCLITR111 Introduction to Literary Studies</b><br>Introduces what literature is, why we read it and how to interpret it. Covers<br>fiction, poetry, drama, non‑fiction and film narration, exploring various<br>literary forms and genres such as graphic narratives and romance novels.

<b>MCCLITR112 Great Literary Works</b><br>Provides a chronological overview of literature from the epic of Gilgamesh to<br>post‑modernity. Reads literary and critical texts that explore human experience<br>and teaches how to approach literature’s ambiguities and trace themes across<br>ages.

<b>MCCLITR211 World Myth & Literature</b><br>Investigates myths from around the world—from Gilgamesh to the Ramayana, Greek<br>and Norse myths. Explores how myths underpin literature and connects them to<br>contemporary global cultures.

<b>MCCLITR212 Life & Travel Writing</b><br>Examines autobiographical and travel writing. Explores how individuals write<br>about self, identity and bodily experience; discusses tropes and models used to<br>represent human experience; and considers memory and imagination in writing.

<b>MCCLITR311 Film & Text</b><br>Studies complex links between literary and film narratives. Analyzes<br>formal aspects of both media, discusses adaptation, intertextuality, viewer<br>participation and narrative dynamics, and allows students to research topics<br>like literature‑to‑film adaptation and cross‑cultural themes.

<b>MCCLITR312 Perspectives on Literary Meaning</b><br>Examines how different perspectives—humanist, feminist, Marxist, cultural<br>minority and psychoanalytic—affect reading and interpretation. Students<br>undertake a research project applying selected perspectives to texts.

<b>MCCMEDI111 Introduction to Film & Media</b><br>Introduces film and media as systems of meaning and cultural production.<br>Examines how images, narratives and technologies shape perception, identity<br>and power; covers film storytelling, representation and genres; and develops<br>critical engagement skills.

<b>MCCMEDI112 Media Archaeology</b><br>Explores media technologies before digital culture. Studies cassette tapes,<br>typewriters and early printing as material objects that carry meaning; includes<br>hands‑on experiments; no technical background required.

<b>MCCMEDI211 From T.V. to TikTok</b><br>Explores how media shape attitudes and provide answers through examples from TV<br>and TikTok. Examines messages that teach fear, pity, admiration and allyship.

<b>MCCMEDI212 Media & the Environment</b><br>Examines representation of environmental concerns through visual culture.<br>Explores the Anthropocene, animal representation, deep time, biocentrism,<br>contested nature, indigenous and postcolonial media; analyzes how media shape<br>environmental understanding; and includes a paper or media project.

<b>MCCMEDI311 Media & Race</b><br>Investigates storytelling and power in relation to race. Examines Afrofuturism<br>and systemic racism and guides students in creating podcasts that explore links<br>between past and present.

<b>MCCMEDI312 The Documentary</b><br>Introduces development of the documentary form. Students write a theoretical<br>paper and produce a short documentary film, fostering understanding of<br>documentary diversity and providing analytical tools for documentary study.

<b>MCCLITR212 Life & Travel Writing</b><br>Examines autobiographical and travel writing. Explores how individuals write<br>about self, identity and bodily experience; discusses tropes and models used to<br>represent human experience; and considers memory and imagination in writing.

<b>MCCLITR311 Film & Text</b><br>Studies complex links between literary and film narratives. Analyzes<br>formal aspects of both media, discusses adaptation, intertextuality, viewer<br>participation and narrative dynamics, and allows students to research topics<br>like literature‑to‑film adaptation and cross‑cultural themes.

<b>MCCLITR312 Perspectives on Literary Meaning</b><br>Examines how different perspectives—humanist, feminist, Marxist, cultural<br>minority and psychoanalytic—affect reading and interpretation. Students<br>undertake a research project applying selected perspectives to texts.

<b>MCCMEDI111 Introduction to Film & Media</b><br>Introduces film and media as systems of meaning and cultural production.<br>Examines how images, narratives and technologies shape perception, identity<br>and power; covers film storytelling, representation and genres; and develops<br>critical engagement skills.

<b>MCCMEDI112 Media Archaeology</b><br>Explores media technologies before digital culture. Studies cassette tapes,<br>typewriters and early printing as material objects that carry meaning; includes<br>hands‑on experiments; no technical background required.

<b>MCCMEDI211 From T.V. to TikTok</b><br>Explores how media shape attitudes and provide answers through examples from TV<br>and TikTok. Examines messages that teach fear, pity, admiration and allyship.

<b>MCCMEDI212 Media & the Environment</b><br>Examines representation of environmental concerns through visual culture.<br>Explores the Anthropocene, animal representation, deep time, biocentrism,<br>contested nature, indigenous and postcolonial media; analyzes how media shape<br>environmental understanding; and includes a paper or media project.

<b>MCCMEDI311 Media & Race</b><br>Investigates storytelling and power in relation to race. Examines Afrofuturism<br>and systemic racism and guides students in creating podcasts that explore links<br>between past and present.

<b>MCCMEDI312 The Documentary</b><br>Introduces development of the documentary form. Students write a theoretical<br>paper and produce a short documentary film, fostering understanding of<br>documentary diversity and providing analytical tools for documentary study.

rect.title: No GATE
